raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) and represents one of the major therapeutic advances in chronic heart failure. Its rationale is biologically complementary: valsartan attenuates maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system activation, while sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, increasing bioavailability of natriuretic peptides and other vasoactive substrates that promote natriuresis, vasodilation, antifibrotic signaling, and reverse remodeling. The angiotensin receptor blocker component was supported by earlier heart-failure evidence with valsartan [1]. Earlier “vasopeptidase” inhibition with omapatrilat suggested clinical potential but was limited by angioedema, particularly when neprilysin inhibition was combined with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition [2], [3], [4]. LCZ696, later named sacubitril/valsartan, avoided direct ACE inhibition and demonstrated potent neurohormonal and blood-pressure effects in early human studies [5].

The pivotal HFrEF evidence came from PARADIGM-HF, which randomized symptomatic patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40% to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril after run-in periods. The trial was stopped early because ARNI reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization, as well as cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalization, and all-cause mortality [7]. Subsequent analyses showed fewer episodes of clinical deterioration and need for treatment intensification [8], and reductions in both sudden death and death from worsening heart failure [9]. Importantly, benefits were consistent across older patients [10], across much of the systolic blood-pressure spectrum, although hypotension was more frequent [11], and even among patients receiving lower-than-target doses [12].

Renal and metabolic observations have also shaped use. Compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan slowed decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate despite slightly more albuminuria [13]. In patients with diabetes, it was associated with greater reductions in HbA1c and less initiation of insulin or oral glucose-lowering therapy [14]. Among patients treated with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, severe hyperkalemia appeared less frequent with ARNI than with enalapril [15]. These findings do not remove the need for monitoring renal function and potassium, but they support ARNI as a disease-modifying therapy rather than merely a vasodilator.

Initiation during or soon after hospitalization has become a key implementation question. PIONEER-HF showed that, in stabilized patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan produced greater early reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [16]. Biomarker analyses suggested rapid improvement in myocardial stress and injury markers [17]. TRANSITION supported feasibility of starting therapy before discharge or shortly after discharge [18], while TITRATION informed dose-escalation strategies, particularly for patients naïve to high-dose ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy [19]. In practice, an ACE inhibitor must be stopped for at least 36 hours before ARNI initiation to reduce angioedema risk; no washout is required when switching from an ARB.

Reverse remodeling provides mechanistic plausibility for clinical benefit. In PROVE-HF, reductions in NT-proBNP after sacubitril/valsartan initiation correlated with improvements in LVEF, ventricular volumes, and atrial volumes over 12 months [20]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant improvement in aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril, but it demonstrated favorable changes in ventricular structure and function [21]. Together, these studies reinforce the concept that ARNI favorably modifies cardiac biology beyond symptomatic unloading.

Evidence in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan in HFpEF [6]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested benefit in patients with LVEF below the normal range [22]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicated that benefit is greatest at lower LVEF and attenuates as LVEF rises [23]. PARAGON-HF also suggested larger benefit in women than men [24]. PARAGLIDE-HF extended the signal to patients with mildly reduced or preserved EF after worsening heart failure, showing reduction in natriuretic peptides and supportive clinical trends [25]. Thus, ARNI is most strongly established in HFrEF, with selected use in HFmrEF and lower-range HFpEF.

Sacubitril/valsartan has not proven broadly beneficial immediately after myocardial infarction without established chronic HFrEF. PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death, incident heart failure, or outpatient heart failure compared with ramipril after acute myocardial infarction, although event patterns were directionally favorable [26]. Current guidelines therefore prioritize ARNI for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, recommend it as preferred renin–angiotensin system inhibition when tolerated, and allow consideration in HFmrEF/HFpEF subsets most likely to benefit [27], [28]. Its use now occurs alongside other foundational therapies, including sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, which independently improve outcomes in HFrEF [29], [30]. The practical challenge is no longer whether ARNI works in HFrEF, but ensuring timely initiation, safe titration, affordability, and integration into quadruple therapy.
